title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Manufacturing
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Clop names more than 40 PTC Windchill victims and what it took is your engineering record
items.content_text: The Clop extortion group has listed over 40 organisations on its leak site after a mass data-theft campaign against internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM product lifecycle management platforms, exploiting CVE-2026-12569, an improper input validation flaw allowing arbitrary code execution. Named organisations include Shell, Philips, Fiserv, Zebra, Mindray and Largan Precision. Researchers report affiliates deploying JSP web shells to exfiltrate data, with confirmed victims across manufacturing, automotive, aerospace and retail, and activity running since early June. What was taken is specific to this sector: engineering blueprints, product designs and manufacturing specifications. That is the material a competitor wants and the material that makes a later targeted intrusion into your plant substantially cheaper, because it hands over your process, your tolerances and often your control system architecture in one archive.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Clop leak-site listings — reported by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Listings reported 15 Aug 2026; campaign since early Jun 2026

items.title: Five federal agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers, critical manufacturing named first
items.content_text: The NSA, CISA, FBI, Department of Energy and EPA issued a joint advisory on 19 August warning that threat actors are combining the open-source snap7 and python-snap7 automation libraries with AI-assisted scripting to build custom tools that mimic legitimate OT monitoring solutions. Those tools provide read and write access to Siemens S7 controller memory, configuration data and ladder logic programs over S7comm. Critical manufacturing is named first among the most-targeted sectors, ahead of energy, water, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities. The agencies state that this is an active threat rather than a theoretical one, and that AI-generated exploitation scripts dramatically reduce the expertise and time needed. Actors find exposed or poorly segmented devices with internet scanning services and gain access through default or weakly configured credentials. Affected lines span S7-200, S7-300 including 314, 315 and 317, S7-400, S7-1200 CPUs 1211C through 1217C, and S7-1500 including F-series safety controllers. The agencies assess current activity as reconnaissance and capability development, with read access used to prepare for later write operations.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Joint advisory AA26-231A (NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE, EPA) — corroborated by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security

items.title: Attackers crossed from a wind farm into an unrelated plant over a shared private cellular APN
items.content_text: CERT Polska disclosed on 9 August that attackers reached the industrial control network of a Polish combined heat and power plant serving roughly 50,000 residents by pivoting through a private cellular data network. The intrusion started at an entirely different organisation: an internet-exposed Fortinet VPN and firewall device at a wind farm sharing the same carrier APN. Because the APN was misconfigured to allow arbitrary devices to communicate with one another, the attacker crossed from one operator’s network into another’s controllers. CERT Polska describes this as the first observed real-world use of a private APN as an OT attack vector. The incident occurred on 29 December 2025 and analysis took over three months. The relevance to manufacturers is architectural: private APN and private 5G are being sold into plants for machine connectivity and remote-site telemetry on the premise that they are safer than the public internet, and a flat one is a shared broadcast domain with other subscribers.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CERT Polska disclosure — reported by SecurityWeek, Help Net Security and BleepingComputer
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Incident 29 Dec 2025; disclosed 9 Aug 2026, analysis published 10–11 Aug 2026

items.title: Manufacturing took 747 of 1,140 industrial ransomware incidents in the second quarter
items.content_text: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents involving industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up 12 percent from 1,020 in the first. Manufacturing accounted for 747 of them, roughly 65 percent of the total, with construction at 176, equipment manufacturing at 114 and food and beverage at 70. The analytical point matters more than the count: ransomware operators do not need control system access to disrupt industrial production, because encrypting the IT systems that support the plant — scheduling, planning, shipping, quality records — is regularly sufficient to stop the line. Extortion also continued its shift away from file encryption toward data theft, which changes the calculus around backups. A plant that can restore every server in eight hours has not addressed the leverage created by an attacker who took the design files and never encrypted anything.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Dragos Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis — via Help Net Security

items.title: Claroty finds one in five facility cyber-physical assets a single hop from internet-exposed systems
items.content_text: Team82 analysed more than 750,000 cyber-physical assets across large data centre facilities and found nearly one in five sitting one hop from a system making outbound internet connections. Close to 90 percent of building management systems communicated over insecure protocols and 40 percent ran outdated firmware, with around a third of HVAC and cooling systems one hop from an internet-exposed system. The research is about data centres, but the asset classes are identical to those in a manufacturing plant: power distribution, building management, physical access control, fire protection and process cooling. Plant utilities are frequently owned by facilities rather than by controls engineering, procured on a separate contract, connected by the supplier for remote monitoring, and left out of the OT asset inventory entirely — which is exactly how the one-hop distance gets so short without anyone deciding it should be.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Claroty Team82, State of CPS Security: Data Center Exposures — reported by SecurityWeek

items.title: August ICS Patch Tuesday: maximum-severity missing authentication in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced
items.content_text: Siemens published ten advisories in the August cycle. The most serious, SSA-834709, covers a maximum-severity missing authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices allowing a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with elevated privileges. Siemens also fixed a critical code execution vulnerability in Siveillance Video Management Servers, and high-severity flaws in Solid Edge, Simcenter Nastran, Siemens License Server, Simcenter Femap, Parasolid and Logo! Soft Comfort that can crash applications, execute arbitrary code, elevate privileges, read arbitrary files or leak information. Medium-severity issues were resolved in Ruggedcom devices and Desigo controllers. Schneider Electric published advisories for NetBotz 5 and PowerChute Serial Shutdown, and Phoenix Contact issued one covering multiple PLCnext firmware flaws. Several of the Siemens items are engineering-workstation software rather than plant devices — Solid Edge, Femap, Nastran and Parasolid all run on the machines that also hold your TIA Portal projects.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Siemens ProductCERT SSA-834709, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact advisories — summarised by SecurityWeek

items.title: Cisco ASA and FTD VPN zero-day exploited to reload firewalls, added to CISA KEV
items.content_text: Cisco has patched CVE-2026-20349, a flaw in the remote-access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure Firewall Threat Defense software that attackers are exploiting to force appliances offline. A specially crafted HTTP request causes an unexpected reload and a denial-of-service condition, with no authentication and no user interaction required. Cisco’s PSIRT confirmed active exploitation in August and CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue with a federal remediation deadline of 14 August. Hot fixes cover ASA 9.16, 9.18, 9.20, 9.22, 9.23 and 9.24 and FTD 7.0, 7.2, 7.4, 7.6, 7.7 and 10.0. For manufacturers the operational risk is loss of remote support at the wrong moment: these appliances usually terminate machine-builder and integrator access into the plant, and a line down at 2am with the OEM unable to connect is a longer outage than the firewall reload itself suggests.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Cisco security advisory and CISA KEV catalogue — reported by Help Net Security and SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Exploitation confirmed and KEV listed Aug 2026; reported 13 Aug 2026

items.title: Four more exploited flaws added to KEV on 18 August, including Windows IKE and VMware vCenter
items.content_text: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August: CVE-2026-33824 in Microsoft Internet Key Exchange, CVE-2026-55040 in Microsoft SharePoint, CVE-2026-59310 in Broadcom VMware vCenter and CVE-2026-65400 in Apple macOS. Two further additions followed on 20 August, both in TrueConf Server. For manufacturers, vCenter is the one that changes the risk model: it commonly manages the virtual infrastructure hosting MES, historians, SCADA servers and virtualised engineering workstations, so a compromise there is a hypervisor problem affecting every OT workload on the cluster at once, not an application problem. IKE terminates site-to-site tunnels between plants, to corporate, and to machine builders. SharePoint deserves a second look because standard operating procedures, machine manuals and process documentation are so often stored there and treated as low-sensitivity.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added 18 Aug 2026; two further additions 20 Aug 2026

items.title: CISA publishes an advisory for flaws in Malcolm, its own free OT monitoring suite
items.content_text: Advisory ICSA-26-230-01 covers vulnerabilities in Malcolm, the network traffic analysis suite CISA distributes free for OT and ICS environments, which could allow an attacker to cause a denial-of-service condition or execute arbitrary code. Affected versions are below 26.06.1, below 26.07.0 and up to and including 26.07.1. The same day CISA published ICSA-26-230-02 covering a stack overflow in Siemens Simcenter Nastran that can be triggered when the application binary reads an arbitrary string as a file argument, with remote code execution possible if a user is tricked into running it; Siemens has released updated versions. Malcolm shows up in manufacturing more often than its profile suggests, usually as a pilot a controls engineer or a consultant stood up to demonstrate network visibility before a budget request — sitting on a span port with sight of the whole plant network, and almost never in a patch inventory.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-230-01 and ICSA-26-230-02

items.title: From 11 September 2026 manufacturers must report exploited vulnerabilities within 24 hours
items.content_text: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations take effect on 11 September 2026. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents affecting the security of those products. The timelines are tight: an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware, a full notification within 72 hours, and a final report within 14 days of a corrective measure being available for an actively exploited vulnerability, or within a month for a severe incident. Reporting goes through a single reporting platform to the relevant national CSIRT, with information made available to ENISA at the same time. Two points are routinely missed. The obligations cover products already on the EU market, not just new launches, so legacy product lines are in scope. And if your machines, controllers or embedded software reach EU customers, you are the manufacturer here — this is not only a supplier concern.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: European Commission, Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations

items.title: US and Australian agencies publish guidance on isolating OT and running that way for an extended period
items.content_text: A joint publication from US and Australian agencies sets out how critical infrastructure operators should prepare to isolate vital operational technology and supporting systems from external connectivity, and to keep operating in that isolated state for an extended period rather than the few hours most continuity plans assume. It is guidance and creates no obligation. Its value for a manufacturer is that it converts a claim most plants make confidently — that the line can keep running if corporate is compromised — into a dependency checklist. The items that break first are rarely on the network diagram as control-system dependencies: time synchronisation, Active Directory authentication for HMI logins, licence servers for HMI and historian software, MES order release, and label printing. Several manufacturers have discovered during a real incident that a licence check phoning home was the thing that stopped the line.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Joint US–Australian OT isolation guidance — reported by SecurityWeek
